The U.S. Army detonated nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, potentially sending toxic lead dust and other deadly contaminants spewing across communities and farmland throughout the Mississippi River water basin. Residents, who were first informed last week, had been ordered to evacuate or else shelter in place. “The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts,” says Pat Elder, who tracks how military activity impacts people and the planet at the Military Poisons project. “There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen.”

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.
Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. The detonation will cause a massive blast that could send toxic lead dust spewing across communities, farmland, and potentially into the Mississippi River. The detonation is scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time.
Officials have recommended residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant to evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. Men are being told to — in this farmland area, to bring their cows inside. A number of farmers have said that’s impossible.
Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, told a reporter he plans to go west to escape the toxic plume.
JEREMY ATWATER: But now the winds are changing directions, and it’s going to blow directly south through our town, so I guess we’re going to head west instead.
REPORTER: And what’s out west? Is it hotels? Or is it just —
JEREMY ATWATER: Anything but the bomb. … My primary concern is a lot. I mean, nobody really knows. There’s never been a documented explosion like this, as far as I could find any doing my due diligence digging in the interweb. But it’s just going to be a big problem. It’s going to be a lot of lead poisoning going on.
AMY GOODMAN: The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There’s no safe level of lead exposure. Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women.

In September 2025, Democracy Now! host Amy Goodman sat down with longtime political prisoner and Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier for his first extended television and radio broadcast interview since his release to home confinement in February 2025. Before his commutation by former President Joe Biden, the 82-year-old Peltier spent nearly 50 years behind bars. Peltier has always maintained his innocence for the 1975 killing of two FBI officers. He is expected to serve the remainder of his life sentences under house arrest at the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Nation in Belcourt, North Dakota. In a wide-ranging conversation, we spoke to Peltier about his case, his time in prison, his childhood spent at an American Indian boarding school and his later involvement in the American Indian Movement (AIM) and more.
“We still have to live under that, that fear of losing our identity, losing our culture, our religion,” Peltier says about his continued commitment to Indigenous rights. “The struggle still goes on for me. I’m not going to give up.”

AMY GOODMAN: In this special broadcast, we spend the hour with longtime Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier. Last February, he was released from a federal prison in Florida after spending nearly half a century behind bars for a crime he says he did not commit. President Biden, on his last day in office, commuted Peltier’s life sentence to home confinement. Biden’s decision followed mounting calls by tribal leaders and supporters around the world in a decadeslong, community-led campaign fighting for his freedom.
In the 1970s, Peltier was involved with the American Indian Movement, known as AIM. In 1975, two FBI agents and one young AIM activist were killed in a shootout on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Two AIM members were later arrested for killing the agents. At the trial, the jury acquitted them. Leonard Peltier was arrested later, tried separately and convicted. Peltier has always maintained his innocence.
Notable supporters of Leonard Peltier over the years have included South African President Nelson Mandela, Pope Francis and Amnesty International. Supporters of Peltier say his trial was marked by gross FBI and federal prosecutorial misconduct, including the coercion of witnesses, fabricated testimony and suppressed exculpatory evidence.
After being released in February, Leonard Peltier returned home to live on the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Reservation in Belcourt, North Dakota. On September 12th, Leonard Peltier celebrated his 81st birthday. People gathered throughout the day, visiting him and calling from around the world to celebrate. That night and the next day, we spoke to Leonard Peltier in his living room in his first extended TV/radio broadcast interview since his release from prison.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson and other officials in the state have denounced the violent arrest of a father and daughter by ICE agents on Saturday as they were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Video of the arrest shows masked plainclothes agents dragging a woman off the jetway as she screams for help. Both Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle said ICE carried out the operation without their knowledge. ICE said Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, originally from Mexico, was targeted for overstaying his tourist visa, and that his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, would be charged with assault for allegedly throwing hot coffee at an agent — although witnesses dispute that account.
“This is one of, unfortunately, many thousands of detentions that is happening not only in Washington state, but across the country,” says Josefina Mora-Cheung, director of organizing for the immigrant justice group La Resistencia. “The only path forward is to abolish ICE.”

The United Nations climate summit in Turkey, known as COP31, collapsed on Sunday after nations failed to reach an agreement on a new climate deal. A number of countries opposed the final draft because it made no mention of fossil fuels. Many poorer countries also objected to the lack of financial commitments from richer nations to assist them in adapting to the climate crisis.
“This is not about the Global South begging for assistance and help,” says Filipino climate activist Lidy Nacpil. “The principle is that [wealthy nations] have created this problem, and they have to contribute to the solutions.”
“What we’ve seen over the past decades is the Global North are not delivering on any of their responsibilities,” says Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA. “That’s what’s causing the deadlock. It’s not new to this COP, but it’s becoming increasingly untenable.”
We also speak with two other leading climate justice advocates who attended COP31, Tasneem Essop of Climate Action Network International and Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy of the Marshall Islands.
